CBW DRAC Onaboarding DRAC Primer Session 2026 Welcome to the Canadian Bioinformatics Workshops (CBW) DRAC Primer Session. This hands-on course introduces a shared high-performance computing (HPC) training cluster and the commands needed to run reproducible bioinformatics analyses. You will learn how to register and connect, manage files, transfer data, use software, submit and monitor Slurm jobs, and access interactive computing resources. The workshop finishes with a short bioinformatics challenge. Workshop details Date: Wednesday, October 28, 2026. Audience: CBW participants who are new to Linux or HPC. Platform: DRAC-hosted CBW training cluster. The instructors will provide the registration link and workshop credentials; do not post passwords in shared documents. Before the session Bring a laptop with a working internet connection and an SSH client (Terminal on macOS/Linux, or Windows Terminal/PowerShell with OpenSSH). Obtain the registration URL from the organizers, and register your username, password and email address as instructed. The login host for this workshop is cbw.c3.ca; do not use a personal DRAC cluster account unless instructed. Use the workshop-specific instructions rather than assumptions about other DRAC clusters. HPC infrastructure, registration and login Learning goals By the end of this module, you should be able to describe a training cluster, register for the workshop, and connect through SSH. What is HPC? A high-performance computing (HPC) cluster combines many networked computers. A login node is the entry point for editing files and submitting work; compute nodes execute jobs. A scheduler (Slurm in this workshop) assigns compute resources according to job requirements and policy. Shared storage lets compute nodes access project data. Component Purpose Login node SSH access, lightweight editing, compilation, job submission Compute node CPU and memory resources for running analyses Slurm Queues, allocates and monitors jobs Shared storage Stores data accessible to jobs Important: Do not run computationally intensive analyses on login nodes. Submit batch jobs or request interactive allocations. Register for the workshop Open the registration link provided by the instructors (the address is not included here because it has not yet been confirmed). Register the required username, password and email. Keep your credentials private. Use the workshop account, which may be distinct from a regular DRAC account. Connect by SSH Open Terminal (macOS/Linux) or Windows Terminal / PowerShell with OpenSSH: ssh YOUR_USERNAME@cbw.c3.ca Replace YOUR_USERNAME with the username you registered. Confirm the host key only after verifying the hostname with the instructors, then enter your password when prompted. The password is not shown as you type. Verify where you are: whoami hostname pwd Log out: exit Exercise: first login Connect to cbw.c3.ca. Run whoami, hostname, and pwd. Identify which machine you are on and why intensive computation belongs on compute nodes. Check your understanding whoami prints your login name; hostname prints the machine name; pwd prints your current directory. Exact values depend on your account and the current training infrastructure. Common connection issues Permission denied: Confirm the username and workshop password; do not share credentials. Could not resolve hostname: Check that cbw.c3.ca was entered correctly and that your network can resolve it. Connection timed out: Check connectivity or ask the instructor whether network access is restricted. Next: Learn to navigate and transfer files.

Working with directories and files Learning goals Navigate Linux directories, inspect text files, organize results, and transfer files between your computer and the training cluster. Explore the shell pwd # Where am I? ls # What is here? ls -lah # Include hidden files and sizes cd ~ # Return to home directory mkdir -p cbw-primer # Create a workspace cd cbw-primer Paths beginning with / are absolute; paths relative to your working directory are relative. .. refers to the parent directory and ~ refers to your home directory. Create and inspect files printf 'sample	reads
A	12
B	8
' > counts.tsv cat counts.tsv head -n 2 counts.tsv wc -l counts.tsv cp counts.tsv counts-copy.tsv mv counts-copy.tsv counts-backup.tsv > creates or overwrites a file. Use it carefully. Use >> to append. printf 'C	15
' >> counts.tsv less counts.tsv Press q to exit less. For editing, you can use nano counts.tsv (Ctrl+O to save, Ctrl+X to exit). File transfer from your own computer Run the following commands in a separate terminal on your laptop, not inside the cluster SSH session: # Upload one local file to your cluster home directory rsync -avh ./example.txt YOUR_USERNAME@cbw.c3.ca:~/cbw-primer/ # Download a result from the cluster rsync -avh YOUR_USERNAME@cbw.c3.ca:~/cbw-primer/counts.tsv ./ Change YOUR_USERNAME and local paths as needed. rsync works over SSH and can resume incremental transfers. FileZilla is a graphical alternative: select SFTP, host cbw.c3.ca, port 22, and use your assigned workshop credentials. Exercise Create ~/cbw-primer/results. Create a text file with three sample names, then inspect it with cat and wc -l. Upload a small text file from your laptop using rsync or FileZilla. Download the file back to your laptop. Example commands mkdir -p ~/cbw-primer/results printf 'sample1
sample2
sample3
' > ~/cbw-primer/samples.txt cat ~/cbw-primer/samples.txt wc -l ~/cbw-primer/samples.txt Shared filesystem etiquette Use descriptive filenames. Avoid generating millions of tiny files or copying large datasets unnecessarily. Ask instructors which directories are appropriate for persistent data and temporary job output; filesystem paths and quotas are cluster-specific. Next: Software modules and reproducible environments.

Software environments and reproducibility Learning goals Find available software, load an environment module, and identify the commands and versions used in an analysis. Environment modules Clusters provide software through environment modules. Available applications and versions depend on the training system. module avail module list module spider python # Available on systems using Lmod module load python # If an appropriate Python module is available python --version module list module load modifies your environment (for example PATH) for the current shell. When finished, you can use module unload <module-name> or module purge; module purge may also remove modules needed by other tools, so use it with care. If a command is unavailable, ask the instructors which software stack is installed rather than installing system-wide software. Python virtual environments If Python and the venv module are available: python -m venv ~/cbw-primer/venv source ~/cbw-primer/venv/bin/activate python --version which python python -m pip list deactivate For workshop exercises, use instructor-supplied package versions. Heavy installs or builds should follow cluster policy and generally run off the login node. Inspect versions and paths command -v python python --version module list 2>&1 Record versions, parameters, input filenames, and job scripts so the work can be reproduced. Different modules or virtual environments may produce different results. Containers and workflows Tools such as Apptainer and workflow managers such as Nextflow or Snakemake can help package complex analyses, but only use them if supported by the workshop environment. Do not assume Docker can run on shared HPC nodes. Exercise Display available modules and the currently loaded set. Load an instructor-approved software module and check its version. Identify the executable used by command -v. Explain why recording versions matters when reproducing an analysis. Next: Submit compute jobs using Slurm.
submit-and-monitor-jobs-with-slurm.html
Submit and monitor jobs with Slurm Why use a scheduler? Write a batch script Understand resource requests Monitor and diagnose jobs Interactive allocations JupyterHub Exercise

Submit and monitor jobs with Slurm Why use a scheduler? On HPC, computation is submitted as a job. Slurm reserves cores, memory and time, and executes the job on an allocated compute node rather than on the login node. Write a batch script Create hello.sbatch with nano hello.sbatch and enter: #!/bin/bash #SBATCH --job-name=cbw-hello #SBATCH --time=00:05:00 #SBATCH --cpus-per-task=1 #SBATCH --mem=1G #SBATCH --output=cbw-hello-%j.out set -euo pipefail printf 'Node: '; hostname printf 'Job ID: %s\n' "$SLURM_JOB_ID" date Some training partitions require an explicit --account or --partition; the instructor will supply the correct values if needed. Do not guess account names. Submit and inspect: sbatch hello.sbatch squeue -u "$USER" sacct -j JOB_ID --format=JobID,State,Elapsed,MaxRSS,ExitCode Replace JOB_ID with the ID returned by sbatch. sacct reporting can lag and depends on the cluster’s accounting configuration. Understand resource requests --time specifies the maximum wall-clock time. --cpus-per-task requests CPU cores for one task; requesting more does not automatically parallelize a program. --mem specifies memory for the job on each allocated node. --output sets the standard-output filename; %j expands to the job ID. Request resources based on measured usage instead of reserving much more than necessary. A job may remain PENDING while resources are unavailable. Monitor and diagnose jobs squeue -u "$USER" scontrol show job JOB_ID sacct -j JOB_ID --format=JobID,JobName,State,Elapsed,MaxRSS,ExitCode scancel JOB_ID # Only when you intend to cancel the job If you see OUT_OF_MEMORY or a time-limit failure, inspect logs and resource requests before rerunning. Interactive allocations For short tests and troubleshooting, if allowed by your training partition: salloc --time=00:15:00 --cpus-per-task=1 --mem=1G srun --pty bash hostname exit exit exit releases the interactive shell; leave the allocation shell too when finished. Some clusters configure salloc differently; follow the instructor’s cluster-specific guidance. JupyterHub If the workshop provides JupyterHub, use the verified URL announced by the instructor. Connect with the workshop credentials, select an approved compute profile, and shut down your session after use. Do not assume that the SSH login host is also the JupyterHub host. Exercise Submit hello.sbatch, find its job ID, inspect its output, and report whether the job completed successfully. Discuss why Slurm jobs are preferable to long-running processes on login nodes. Bioinformatics mini-challenge Goal Step 1: Create a sample FASTA file Step 2: Explore the data Step 3: Build a simple analysis script Step 4: Submit the analysis to Slurm Step 5: Save and transfer results Stretch challenge Wrap-up

Bioinformatics mini-challenge Goal Combine shell operations, a small sequence dataset, a reproducible script and a Slurm batch job. All data are generated inside your workspace; no external downloads are required. Step 1: Create a sample FASTA file mkdir -p ~/cbw-primer/challenge cd ~/cbw-primer/challenge cat > sequences.fa <<'EOF' >seqA ACGTACGT >seqB GGGTTT >seqC ATATATATAT EOF FASTA records begin with > followed by an identifier and one or more sequence lines. Step 2: Explore the data head sequences.fa grep -c '^>' sequences.fa wc -l sequences.fa Question: How many sequences are present? Why is wc -l not always a reliable sequence counter for FASTA? Answer There are 3 sequences. FASTA sequences can occupy multiple lines, so counting total lines does not count records reliably. Counting header lines beginning with > is appropriate for well-formed FASTA. Step 3: Build a simple analysis script Save the following as analyze.sh: #!/bin/bash set -euo pipefail input="${1:?Usage: bash analyze.sh INPUT.fa}" printf 'Input: %s\n' "$input" printf 'Sequences: ' grep -c '^>' "$input" printf 'Total bases: ' awk '!/^>/ {gsub(/[[:space:]]/, ""); n += length($0)} END {print n+0}' "$input" Run it: bash analyze.sh sequences.fa Expected results: 3 sequences and 24 bases. The base count sums sequence-line lengths and supports wrapped FASTA records. Step 4: Submit the analysis to Slurm Save as analyze.sbatch: #!/bin/bash #SBATCH --job-name=fasta-count #SBATCH --time=00:05:00 #SBATCH --cpus-per-task=1 #SBATCH --mem=1G #SBATCH --output=fasta-count-%j.out set -euo pipefail cd "$SLURM_SUBMIT_DIR" bash analyze.sh sequences.fa Run: sbatch analyze.sbatch squeue -u "$USER" Once it finishes, inspect the fasta-count-JOBID.out file (replace JOBID with the actual number). If your training allocation requires --account or --partition, use the instructor-provided values. Step 5: Save and transfer results From your laptop, retrieve the output with rsync (substitute the job ID and workshop username): rsync -avh YOUR_USERNAME@cbw.c3.ca:~/cbw-primer/challenge/fasta-count-JOBID.out ./ Stretch challenge Modify analyze.sh to accept multiple FASTA files, using a for filename in "$@" loop. Consider how you would process hundreds of files using a Slurm job array rather than running one long serial task. Wrap-up You have registered and logged in to an HPC training cluster, organized data, used environment modules, submitted and inspected a job, and run a reproducible bioinformatics script. For production work, benchmark resource usage and use the official cluster documentation and policies.
